We are here this morning to recognize Detective Taylor HART for our September officer of the month, 2026. Taylor has been with the Tampa Police Department 15 years and served 6 yores as a detective. His exceptional investigative work targeting and dismantling major drug trafficking organizations responsible for distributing dangerous narcotics throughout the Tampa Bay area. He is assigned to the high intensity drug trafficking area task force and serving as task force officer with homeland security investigations. He handles complex, long-term investigations focused on drug traffickers, distributors and sources of supply. As lead detective in a multistate drug traffic investigation, detective HART helped dismantle major narcotics distribution network operating throughout Hillsborough and pasco counties. The investigation resulted in 6 federal indictments, removal of large quantities of narcotics from our community. Those convicted received significant federal prison sentences including one sentence of 20 years. In a separate investigation targeting major fentanyl traffic organization, detective HART worked alongside state and federal partners to identify key traffickers, disrupt their service supply. Investigation resulted in 7 search warrants, 12 arrest warrants and seizure of significant amount of fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, firearms and $25,000 in currency. Related investigation led to prosecution of major fentanyl supplier who faced a 27-year prison sentence. His investigative work helped take dangerous drugs off the streets, held high level traffickers accountable and dismantled supply of narcotics in the region. We would like to recognize him as the September officer of the month. [ applause ]

segments.text: Thank you very much. Martin followed by edward followed by Stephen Michelini. Dr. Huff, I saw you fill out a card. We'll be doing board appointments after public comments. Martin, start with your name, please. I live on watrous avenue. Professional engineer, geotechnical engineer. Ben practicing in the Tampa Bay area for 40 years. In order to approve this project, you've got to trust the engineering. So I want to talk about the engineering features. This project includes 5,000 linear feet of street, excavation 15 to 19 feet deep and is going to open up Howard Avenue for four years. We lose Howard Avenue for four years. I've been told that Howard Avenue needs to suck it up and every other neighborhood has dealt with this. That's not true. Typically, stormwater project, you might have ten foot deep excavations. This project is going to have an excavation as wide as this room and probably seven to eight feet higher than the ceiling right here. You don't do that with a trench box. Trench box is a conventional method for shoring up smaller excavations. Totally inadequate. Trench box about this wide, perhaps 10 to 20 feet long and maybe this high. It's not going to do the job. That is absolutely not going to happen, won't do the job whatsoever. We looked at the geology of this. It's hard to see here. This is the box culvert bottom right there. Right at the bottom of the box culvert, you have very hard rock. This is from soil borings done. You cannot drive any piles into that hard rock. What you'll need to shore up the excavation is not a trench box. Typically what you do is you do sheet piling and embed the sheet piling like one and a half to two times deeper than the excavation. Here is the sheet piling. You drive it down. It's embedded. When the pressure pushes on it, it's strong enough to resist. In this case, you drive the sheet piling, hits the rock, can't go any deeper. 12,000 pounds per linear foot hits this, it fails. Sheet piling is not going to work. The other alternative is, you might want to do internal bracing. Can't do it. You have to get a 10-foot culvert in there and it's not going to fit. Another way, tiebacks. You won't get permission from the property owners because they do not like this project. The other way that will certainly work would be a combination wall. Drilled shafts about every ten feet. They talked about the 60% plans. There's no shoring in the 60% plans. I looked at the line items that get you up to 92.5 million. There's no shoring in that. I'd love to have more time. But I get it.

segments.text: Thank you. Harry, followed by rumela das. Harry Coleman. I live in Parkland Estates. I'm speaking today on behalf of support of items 36 through 39, South Howard flood relief project. segments.text: Thank you, Sir. Tyler, start with your name, please. You have three minutes. Followed by clarence and followed by gloria sims. Tyler rorrer. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. I'm here representing a local running community in the Tampa Bay area. Our running community has grown tremendously. Run clubs have become places where people get healthy, make friends, and build community. Our club regularly brings together 150 to 250 people for a single run. Running is one of the most accessible forms of exercises. You need a pair of shoes and a safe place to run. That's where Tampa has a gap. Tampa does not currently have a dedicated municipal running track that residents can simply access as a public recreational amenity. We have parks trails, pools, and basketball courts. But if I wanted a structured running workout on safe, flat, measured surface, there isn't a public track that I can simply use. We're not asking for a track to host track meets. I want to make sure that's clear. But track is recreational infrastructure. It gives beginners a place to walk, jog, kids a place to run, seniors a place to exercise, and athletes a place to train. For large run clubs, it's also a safer alternative than putting 158 to 200 people in the roadway. Raleigh, North Carolina, operates a quarter mile track as part of the municipal athletic park system. Nashville has incorporated a public track into the athletic complex. We're not asking Tampa to invent something. We're asking Tampa to look at models that other cities are already using. We see two opportunities here. First, Hillsborough County Public Schools already has tracks throughout our community. I researched the current rental cost for Jefferson high school track. segments.text: Unanimous consent to address item 44? Item number 44. Any staff here? Hello there. Caught me off guard there for a second. Good afternoon. Dave hay, Planning Commission staff. Before I begin the presentation, I want to acknowledge Danny Collins who was instrumental in the Planning Commission's research and coordination with City staff. He is enjoying a well-deserved vacation, so you are all stuck with me this afternoon. I'll be presenting with the assistance of City Planning and legal staff, and we will be presenting the results of the research conducted regarding your motion. As a reminder, your motion asked us to research ways other local governments restrict comprehensive plan amendments to the entitlements approved in a Planned Development rezoning and to outline the impacts of using similar approaches here in Tampa. To frame the discussion, we'll start with Florida's growth management requirements. State law is very clear in this. Each future land use category must be defined in terms of uses included and must include standards to be followed in the control and distribution of population densities and building and structure intensities. This means any PD future land use category must still include defined standards, density, intensity, and allowable uses within the comprehensive plan itself, a PD zoning condition alone cannot substitute for this statutory requirements. In Florida, PD flu categories are most commonly used for large, undeveloped tracts, often master planned communities. They provide flexibility for unique site conditions and long-term development programs. A good example here is pasco county starkey ranch subarea which is around 2,000 acres. These PD flu designations are typically paired with detailed development standards adopted directly into the comprehensive plan. Tampa's development pattern is very different to pasco's. We currently have 26 flu categories, all of which include defined uses, density, and f.a.r., floor area ratio maximums. We do not have a PD flu category or similar mechanism currently. Importantly, the median comprehensive plan amendment in Tampa is about 1.02 acres in size. That's a very small scale compared to the large tracts of PD flu categories typically used elsewhere. The team reviewed several jurisdictions, pasco county was one of them. Seminole county, orange county, and the city of gainesville. Each uses PD flu categories differently. But the common theme is that they apply them to large areas and rely on multiple layers of approval. Map amendments, text amendments, PD zonings, and any adopting ordinances. Across jurisdictions we found several consistent patterns. Many require both a map and text amendment adopted by ordinance. Most apply the PD flu categories to large undeveloped land. Several jurisdictions are moving away from this mechanism due to complexity and notably cities like Orlando, miami, and ft. Lauderdale do not use PD flu categories at all. Overall, PD flu categories tend to add complexity rather than reduce them is what staff found in our discussions with the other jurisdictions. Here is an example from one of pasco's 86 master planned unit developments or subareas. You could see it calls out specific maximums for each approved use. The actual design guidelines for any of the area would be further regulated through pasco's land development code. All right. Staff found that Tampa already has several tools that provide flexibility without needing Planned Development flu category. First, development bonuses allow projects to exceed standard density or f.a.r. When they provide public benefit such as affordable housing contributions, transit, or infrastructure improvements. This gives applicants a predictable path to additional intensity and density, while ensuring the city receives something in return. The second, adaptive reuse incentives support redevelopment of older or historic buildings. These incentives already apply within urban villages and are proposed for expansion citywide. They allow projects to consider uses or f.a.r. Levels that normally wouldn't be permitted under the underlying flu category which is especially helpful for infill sites. Third, expanding flexible categories like the existing neighborhood mixed use future land use categories can support mixed use redevelopment without requiring PD zonings or a new flu designation. Finally, the city can initiate publicly initiated map amendments for unique sites where the existing flu may not align with development goals. This keeps the process predictable while still allowing for some flexibility. Together, these tools already provide multiple pathways for flexibility in redevelopment without introducing an additional layer of review that a PD flu category would potentially require. Overall, the staff found that introducing a PD flu category in Tampa would potentially create several challenges to how the system operates. At first, there is the issue of consistency with Florida's comprehensive Planning requirements. State law requires every flu category to include those defined standards for uses, density, intensity. A PD flu category can't rely solely on the PD zonings that are attached to it, the conditions in that zoning. Those standards must be written directly into the comprehensive plan. That's to meet state law. That means that each PD project would need its own set of site-specific standards adopted through a text amendment. Which that text amendment would need to be reviewed by the state. Second, this creates a more complex approval structure that the staff found instead of just a map amendment with an associated rezoning, like I had said earlier, it will require three separate actions. The flu map changed to actually change the subject site from the flu category now to the PD flu designation. A comprehensive plan text amendment associated with that, that would establish the project's maximum entitlements under that specific PD flu. And then the PD zoning itself would also need to be processed for zoning. Third, this PD flu approach requires a mechanism in the comprehensive plan to track and maintain project's specific entitlements over time. Tampa processes a high volume of small infill amendments, typically slightly over an acre. Adding project-specific flu standards for each of those sites would significantly increase, or potentially increase, administrative complexity. Fourth, it would significantly increase staff workload and review timelines because each PD flu designation, since it would carry its own site-specific requirements, staff would need to prepare, review, and maintain a growing list because if like in pasco there's 86, they started out with one and then it eventually starts building. Fifth it may reduce the overall transparency and predictability for everyone involved in the development process. Right now -- and you all know this -- you know, you can go into the comprehensive plan and look at, okay, this neighborhood is r-10. There's going to be fluctuations in the zoning underneath that, but they are all capped at the 10. Under this potential PD flu, you could get things that are slightly -- if you all agree -- slightly over ten or it could be under 10, but a citizen would need to research the PD flu because now since it will now not show on the map as the entitlement. There is that complexity in it. Finally, adopting the PD flu category could work against one of the city's stated goals through the land development code update, the city has been emphasizing reducing the reliance on PD zoning in favor of more predictable form based and conventional zoning tool. A PD flu category would likely increase the number of those PD zonings, not decrease them, because applicants would need to do an additional PD. They could not do a euclidean under the PD flu category. Together, it was staff's finding that these issues show that the challenges are not just procedural. They affect clarity, predictability and long-term administration. When combined with the structural concerns we discussed in a couple of slides back, they suggest that a PD flu category may introduce some more complex issues than the overall benefit in Tampa's ongoing redevelopment. Here we've got South Tampa Ballast Point. You know how the structure works. Basically, the adopted flu guides the zoning districts that contain more detail than what the comp plan does. They can't exceed what this map says. What staff found was that over time, the potential, all the yellows, these are PD zonings. It would eventually, how the zoning map looks here could eventually how this flu map could eventually look with these kind of PD holes in them that then would require further research on what the entitlements were underneath that particular flu. Overall, there were just some considerations. If you all do decide to move this forward, it would be one of the recommendations from the Planning Commission that we look at the cost of what the impacts potentially could be with implementing this. In conclusion, our team did find that the PD flu categories are typically used for those large tracts of undeveloped land, often 50 acres or more. Tampa's development pattern is, again, fundamentally different. Most amendments involve small -- currently, most amendments involve those small infill sites. Staff found that it potentially could increase the number of amendments, extend the review timelines because now you would technically need to go to the state for the text amendment, the associated text amendment. It may also conflict with the stated goal that I know we've all been kind of working toward of reducing the PD zoning. Given these factors and the other tools such as the bonuses and the adaptive reuse incentives that are currently on there in the comp plan update that hopefully you all see shortly and target amendments that you all can initiate if there are areas where you feel that the comp plan is not in alignment with where the city would like to go. Those tools provide greater flexibility with fewer administrative burdens is what staff found. So that concludes my presentation. I know I'm available and City staff is here as well if you have any questions or concerns. Thank you.

That was added to ensure that we are doing everything we can to minimize the impacts to the businesses on South Howard and on swann. So we will cover that in a little bit. Next slide, please. This is the proposed flooding solution. Its primary feature is 10 by 10 gravity box, culvert terminating at the AMI pond. It includes secondary pipelines that connect the selmon expressway and also a 72-inch pipeline that connects Parkland Estates. This is a legacy project that will serve other neighborhoods in the future that flood east and of West Howard Avenue. You cannot do that with a force main. If you were to build a force main alternative, you are locked in. Locked in to what you can tie into that. So I want to cover the AMI pond. Going back to the AMI pond, I would like to clear up a few misconceptions. First, it is a pond, not a vault. So it has a dirt bottom. It is not silted in. You've heard that the AMI pumping station hasn't worked in ten years. The existing pumping station works. In fact, our computer modeling system called SCADA shows that the two pumps at the station automatically turned on and turned off 177 times over the last 90 days. It works just fine. So the statement that this pump station hasn't worked in ten years is blatantly false. It pumps water to the cleveland system to the west and outfalls three miles away to Old Tampa Bay. It just so happens -- well, let me back up. This level storm is the city's standard engineering design storm and it's for which we design other projects for. So what does this mean? Equivalent of 5.3 inches of rain over an 8-hour period. It just so happens we had a storm with identical characteristics with 5.4 inches of rain on August 1st, 2015. What did it look like? Two bus service route interruptions, route 14 and route 19. Lost business revenue on Swann Avenue and, of course, costly repairs. Fast-forward to a month ago, we had a storm that was smaller, a smaller storm. Only a two-inch storm, with shorter duration. This is what Parkland Estates looked like one month ago. What does this investment of $100 million deliver? 95% flood reduction in Palma Ceia Pines and Parkland Estates. Yes, in Palma Ceia Pines. So you've heard many, many times, it does not provide -- phase one does not provide flood relief to Palma Ceia Pines. That is false. It does provide significant relief to Palma Ceia Pines. No structural flooding for the design storm in either Palma Ceia Pines or Parkland Estates. And approximately 230 homes, you've heard different numbers. You heard 220, 225, 235. It's 230, plus or minus, homes and businesses would have been spared by milton. If you recall, we had in the neighborhood of 330 homes that flooded -- homes and businesses that flooded during milton. All right. This is where I need Brandon's help. This is before on the left and after the 10 by 10 box. He's going to pause at five hours. And that is when the flooding has peaked. Drainage project and fixing the chronic flooding we see in Parkland Estates, Palma Ceia Pines and the nearby neighborhoods. The root of the problem is pretty simple: these neighborhoods sit very, very low. Because of that low-lying topography, they are especially prone to flooding. These neighborhoods are also shaped like giant bowls, when heavy rain hits, water rushes in, fills up fast and doesn't drain the way it should because current pipes there are way too small. City engineers and independent experts are designing this system to handle a serious storm, about five inches of rain over eight hours. That's enough water to fill the iconic river gate tower. When all that water has nowhere to go it can cause a lot of damage. So what is the fix? The proposed solution uses a massive 10-foot by 10-foot box culvert system capable of moving roughly 20 million gallons of stormwater every single hour. Think of it as a mile-long underground river designed to pull all that excess water out of these neighborhoods. The system would start near South Howard and Bayshore, head north, turn onto Swann Avenue, and then continue north into Palma Ceia Pines by connecting directly to the pond beneath the hca Florida South Tampa hospital parking deck. That pond would essentially become a giant inlet pulling excess floodwater out of the neighborhood and sending it south where it can drain properly. Remember the sheer volume of water we're talking about, beer can building worth, the system is designed to move it out of the neighborhoods fast before it can cause serious damage. This approach isn't new. In fact, it's tried and true. Similar projects across the city including at Henderson and dale mabry are already proving how effective this type of drainage system can be. Bottom line, less flooding means safer streets for everyday drivers and first responders, fewer homes at risk of catastrophic damage, lower insurance costs, and real peace of mind for families and businesses who just want to know their investments are better protected.
